You’ve mentioned you’ve been growing basil, mint, and cherry tomatoes, and you’ve used mixed greens and quinoa salads before — here are several dinner ideas that highlight those homegrown ingredients and would work well for a family gathering this weekend:

- Tomato–Basil Caprese Platter: Halve your cherry tomatoes, layer with fresh mozzarella (or burrata), plenty of torn basil, a drizzle of good olive oil and balsamic, and finish with salt and pepper. Serve as a shared starter.

- Basil Pesto Pasta (crowd-friendly): Make a big batch of basil pesto with your basil, olive oil, garlic, Parmesan, and toasted pine nuts (or walnuts). Toss with pasta and roast cherry tomatoes (or add them fresh) and serve family-style.

- Quinoa Salad with Roasted Veg & Greens: Build on the quinoa salad you liked — roast cherry tomatoes and other veg, toss with quinoa, mixed greens, chopped basil, a lemon–olive oil vinaigrette, and optional toasted nuts or feta for texture.

- Herb-Marinated Grilled Chicken or Fish: Marinate chicken breasts or fillets in lemon, olive oil, chopped basil and mint, garlic, salt and pepper, then grill. Serve sliced over mixed greens or alongside the pesto pasta/roasted veg.

- Tomato Galette or Tart: Use a sheet of puff pastry or savory crust, spread a thin layer of herbed ricotta (mix ricotta with chopped basil and a little lemon), top with halved cherry tomatoes and bake until golden — easy to slice and share.

- Yogurt–Mint Sauce / Raita: Make a simple yogurt sauce with chopped mint, lemon juice, salt, and a little garlic or cucumber. It’s a fresh, cool condiment for grilled meats, roasted veg, or to dollop on the quinoa salad.

Menu idea for a balanced family dinner: Caprese platter to start, pesto pasta and a large quinoa + roasted veg salad as mains, grilled herb chicken or fish for protein, with yogurt–mint sauce on the side — finish with a simple dessert (fresh fruit or a light espresso dessert if you want to showcase your espresso interest).

Here are practical tips, drawing on the points you’ve already discussed about Stratocasters and Les Pauls and getting a good sound in alternate tunings:

- Decide what styles you want to play. Your choice (e.g., Strat vs Les Paul) will affect tone: the Les Paul gives a thicker, warmer, sustain-heavy sound good for rock/lead work, while Strats (single-coil) are brighter and more chimey.

- Body & construction: Les Pauls are typically set-neck, mahogany bodies with a maple top (heavier, more sustain). Strats are usually bolt-on and contoured (lighter, snappier). Consider weight and feel in the store.

- Pickups and tonal flexibility: Humbuckers (common on Les Pauls) deliver a fuller, chunkier tone; single-coils (Strat) are clearer. If you want more tones, look for coil-splitting/coil-tap options or a guitar with mixed pickup configurations.

- Neck and playability: Try neck profiles and fretboard radii in person — comfort matters for fingerpicking, chords, and fast runs. If you plan acoustic-like fingerpicking (e.g., “Blackbird”-style), test the guitar unplugged and plugged in to judge how well it responds to light, articulate playing.

- Setup for alternate tunings: If you plan to use open D or lower tunings, consider heavier strings (e.g., .012+), check that the guitar’s setup (action, intonation) can be adjusted, and be prepared to have a tech tweak the nut/truss rod if needed for lower tensions.

- Electronics & hardware check: Plug the guitar into an amp you like, listen for crackle in pots/switches, test all pickup positions, and check tuner stability and bridge function.

- Frets, finish, and buzzing: Play across the fretboard for dead frets, buzzing, and overall fret condition. Check neck relief and action for comfort.

- Weight & balance: Especially for Les Pauls (can be heavy), make sure it balances well sitting and standing.

- Accessories & extras: Ask about warranty, whether it includes a setup, and factor in costs for a professional setup, preferred strings, and a case.

- Try combinations through an amp: Bring or use a clean/dirty amp to hear how the guitar behaves with different gain levels and to judge sustain and clarity.

If you tell me what genres you play most and whether you prefer single-coil sparkle or humbucker thickness, I can suggest specific models or features to prioritize.
